content.content:
1	Temperature-sensitive goods such as vaccines, biological samples, prepared meals and laboratory reagents are frequently shipped in insulated carriers that hold a payload within a target temperature band for a period of hours or days. Carriers of this general kind fall into two broad families. Powered carriers use a fan, a pump or another driven air mover, together with a power source, to force air over a cold source and through the payload space. Passive carriers omit the power source and rely on conduction from, and natural convection around, a refrigerant mass such as water ice, dry ice, gel packs or sealed cassettes charged with a phase-change material.
2	
3	Passive carriers are attractive because they have no battery to charge, no motor to fail and no electrical approval burden for air transport. They are also harder to control. When a refrigerant mass is simply laid on top of, beside or beneath a payload, the cooled air falls where gravity and the packing arrangement happen to send it. Items directly against the refrigerant are driven toward the cold end of the acceptable band or below it, while items on the far side of the payload sit in a stagnant warm layer. The result is a temperature spread across the payload that grows as the load is packed more densely, and that varies from shipment to shipment because it depends on how a particular packer arranged the goods and the refrigerant on a particular day.
4	
5	Attempts to impose a defined circulation path on a passive carrier run into a practical difficulty. The path is defined by clearances, by openings and by the alignment between them, and every one of those relationships is destroyed if the component that carries the openings is set down rotated, offset or skewed by a person working quickly at a packing bench. A carrier that circulates air well when it is assembled precisely, and poorly when it is not, delivers the variability it was intended to remove. Packing instructions, printed arrows and keyed corner blocks all depend on the packer looking, and none of them acts on a component that has already been set down out of position.
6	
7	Two further problems attend repeated reuse of a passive carrier. First, moist ambient air admitted each time the carrier is opened condenses on the cold surfaces of the refrigerant mass and runs down into the payload space, wetting labels and cartons and, over many cycles, leaving standing water in the base of the carrier. Where the refrigerant is a sealed cassette, drying the interior often means removing the cassette from service. Second, a passive carrier gives no account of itself. If the payload was exposed to a temperature excursion in transit, and the refrigerant has since recovered, an inspection at the receiving dock shows a cold carrier and a firm cassette, and the excursion leaves no trace. Electronic data loggers record such events but add cost, battery management and a reading step to every unit shipped, and they report a sensor location rather than the state of the refrigerant that the payload actually depends on.
8	
9	There remains a need for a reusable passive carrier that establishes the same circulation path around the payload every time it is closed, without a powered air mover and without relying on the care of the person who packed it, that manages the condensate produced by repeated opening without taking the refrigerant out of service, and that retains a visible mechanical record of a refrigerant temperature excursion after the refrigerant has recovered.
10

input.summary:
Ledger scope: the sole inventor authority is the single USER passage (input/disclosure.md, reproduced as conversation.md lines 7-17). The only other conversation turn is labeled "YOU (the drafting agent)" (conversation.md line 21) and was treated as candidate prose, not support. input/brief.md was used only for title, applicant/inventor, no-priority and no-government-support formalities; 01-title, 02-cross-reference and 03-government-support match it.

Traced and supported: shell/floor/side walls/upper edge; removable tray with bottom wall, tray side walls, feet on the floor, lower return passage, side supply passages, perforations; module = rigid spacer frame + two opposed cassettes, resting above tray and below lid; central inlet opening opening downward into the central space between confronting faces; two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes; peripheral outlet openings aligned/overlapping the side supply passages; the whole circulation path and the "free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover" limitation; depending indexing rib entering the mating channel and shifting the module into the registered position, with the gasket sealing only after registration (which also supports the pre-seating engagement of claim 12 and description para. 21); resilient feet pressed against shell ledges so the module cannot lift from the tray; shallow condensate channel around the tray, removable wick, discharge openings at guide-duct lower ends, pull tab accessible with the tray out, replacement without opening a cassette; mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside with stem thermally coupled to one cassette, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position surviving recovery, manual reset only after opening, and no control of airflow; the Operation sequence; and the optional-feature statement. Claim 5 traces to "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame"; claim 15 traces to a depending rib entering a channel from above.

Internal consistency checks that passed: claims, Summary, Abstract and Detailed Description use the same terms and relationships as the disclosure (aligned/overlap, registered position, lower return passage, side supply passages); every numeral in draft/numerals.md is used once and for one part only, and tray feet 22 are kept distinct from resilient feet 58; the FIG. 1 section plane ("transversely to the two phase-change cassettes and through the mating channel") is geometrically consistent with the left/right and upper/lower placement of the FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 fragments and with FIG. 2's wall assignments; the three broken-line enlargement curves carry the same designations in FIG-1.md, in the Brief Description and in each enlargement brief; the section line is designated "7-7" identically in FIG-6.md (repeated at both ends, both arrows one way), in FIG-7.md and in both Brief Description sentences, and the FIG. 7 view direction is consistent with the FIG. 6 arrow direction; no drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction or unresolved alternative remains anywhere in draft/ or figures/. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no documents and the Background cites none, so there is nothing to trace in the citation channel; the Background's generic powered/passive-carrier characterizations need no inventor support.

Three defects found. One is critical: FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 verbalize the tray side wall's lower edge as "spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough" / "spaced above the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough". No inventor passage describes a lower edge, its spacing, or its position relative to the condensate channel, and the spacing opens a gap by which the side supply passage reaches the space beneath the tray without passing the perforations 30, contradicting the one disclosed route recited in claims 1, 13 and 17. The only text describing that choice is the drafting agent's own turn. One is major: FIG. 2 asserts the mating channel is a groove "running across the wall thickness", an untraced runout statement on the registration joint that also sits awkwardly against FIG. 3's matched-width, in-contact fit for the same groove. One is minor: FIG. 2 depicts the guide-duct channels and the through opening at each channel's foot but neither the brief's numeral list nor the FIG. 2 Brief Description designates them 50 and 76, though the same structures are designated in FIG. 4, FIG. 5 and the Detailed Description. Each finding carries a drop-in fix; no fix adds any speculative shape or optional embodiment to the application text.

findings.title: Untraced tray-wall lower-edge geometry in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 opens an undisclosed bypass around the perforations
findings.where: figures/FIG-1.md line 7; figures/FIG-5.md line 9 (and the dependent wording in figures/FIG-4.md line 15)
findings.detail: Both briefs verbalize the level of the tray side wall's lower edge and its position relative to the condensate channel. The disclosure discloses only that the tray is "suspended above the shell floor by feet", that the side supply passages are formed between the tray side walls and the shell side walls, and that air "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage". There is no affirmative passage describing a lower edge of the tray side wall, its spacing above the floor, or its position immediately inboard of the trough. These are relative locations on a flow boundary and are therefore substantive even in a schematic section. They also do technical work in the wrong direction: a lower edge spaced above the floor leaves an open gap by which the side supply passage 28 communicates with the space beneath the tray without passing through the perforations 30, so the depicted structure gives the perforations no function and departs from the single circulation path recited in claims 1, 13 and 17 and in draft/08-detailed-description.md line 9 ("Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24"). The only text that describes this arrangement is the drafting agent's own turn at input/conversation.md line 21, which is labeled YOU and is not inventor support.
findings.evidence: Candidate, FIG-1.md line 7: "and continue below the bottom wall to a lower edge spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough, the tray carried by the tray feet 22, small openings through that lower portion connecting each gap with the space beneath the tray". Candidate, FIG-5.md line 9: "its lower edge spaced above the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough described below". Nearest source passages, disclosure.md line 5: "The product tray is suspended above the shell floor by feet so that a lower return passage remains under the tray." and line 7: "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage." No affirmative passage mentions the tray wall's lower edge, its spacing above the floor, or the trough's position relative to it. Non-source origin, conversation.md line 21 (YOU): "FIG. 1 now shows each tray wall continuing below the bottom wall to a lower edge spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough ... so the brief no longer asserts contact with the floor or that the perforations are the only route."
findings.fix: In figures/FIG-1.md line 7, replace "and continue below the bottom wall to a lower edge spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough, the tray carried by the tray feet 22, small openings through that lower portion connecting each gap with the space beneath the tray" with "and continue below the bottom wall down to the floor 12, the tray carried by the tray feet 22, small openings through that lower portion connecting each gap with the space beneath the tray". In figures/FIG-5.md line 9, replace "a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the left of the inner surface of the upright wall body, its lower edge spaced above the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough described below." with "a thin hatched upright wall is drawn in section, spaced to the left of the inner surface of the upright wall body and continuing down to the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body." Leave figures/FIG-4.md, the Brief Description, the Detailed Description, the claims and the numeral table unchanged; the perforations then remain the depicted communication between the side supply passage 28 and the space beneath the tray, as disclosed, and no statement about edge spacing or trough-relative position remains.

findings.title: FIG. 2 asserts an untraced runout for the mating channel groove, and the assertion strains against FIG. 3's fit for the same groove
findings.detail: FIG. 2 states that the mating channel groove runs across the thickness of the near long side wall, i.e. that it runs out at both the inboard and the outboard face of that wall. The disclosure says only that "the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position". Nothing describes the groove's extent or its runout. Runout direction on a registration slot is expressly substantive geometry, because the directions in which the groove can constrain and shift the frame are what make the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The statement also constrains the same groove differently from FIG. 3, which is a section on a plane cutting across that wall and which fixes the groove's width to the rib's thickness with the two in contact; satisfying both briefs forces an undisclosed equality between the rib thickness and the side wall thickness. The Detailed Description and claim 15 are correctly shape-neutral ("opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame"), so the defect is confined to the figure brief and can be removed there.
findings.evidence: Candidate, FIG-2.md line 15: "The top edge of the near long side wall carries an upwardly open groove running across the wall thickness. This groove is the mating channel 56." Competing candidate, FIG-3.md line 13: "Its upper edge carries an upwardly open groove whose width matches the thickness of the depending indexing rib 62 and which receives the lower end of that rib, the two in contact." Nearest source passage, disclosure.md line 9: "As the lid closes, the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position in which the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages." No affirmative passage describes the groove's extent, runout or fit.

This groove is the mating channel 56." with "The top edge of the near long side wall carries a narrow upwardly open groove, shown schematically. This groove is the mating channel 56." Make no change to figures/FIG-3.md, the Brief Description, the Detailed Description or claim 15.

findings.title: FIG. 2 depicts the guide ducts and their lower-end discharge openings but designates neither, unlike FIG. 4, FIG. 5 and the Detailed Description
findings.where: figures/FIG-2.md lines 8, 11 and the "Numerals shown on this figure" list; draft/07-drawings.md line 3
findings.detail: FIG. 2 draws the channel between each cassette and the adjacent long side wall, and a through opening down through the bottom panel at the foot of each channel. Those are the same structures the Detailed Description and the other briefs designate guide ducts 50 and discharge openings 76, yet FIG. 2 leaves both unnamed and unnumbered, and the FIG. 2 sentence of the Brief Description omits them, while draft/08-detailed-description.md line 15 sends the reader only to FIG. 4 for the guide ducts. A reader of the module view therefore cannot tie the channels or the openings at their feet to any numeral, even though both structures are disclosed ("two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes"; "Openings at the lower ends of the guide ducts discharge condensate into the channel"). Traced and supported: shell/floor/side walls/upper edge; removable tray with bottom wall, tray side walls, feet on the floor, lower return passage, side supply passages, perforations; module = rigid spacer frame + two opposed cassettes, resting above tray and below lid; central inlet opening opening downward into the central space between confronting faces; two downward guide ducts beside the cassettes; peripheral outlet openings aligned/overlapping the side supply passages; the whole circulation path and the "free of a fan, a pump and any powered air mover" limitation; depending indexing rib entering the mating channel and shifting the module into the registered position, with the gasket sealing only after registration (which also supports the pre-seating engagement of claim 12 and description para. 21); resilient feet pressed against shell ledges so the module cannot lift from the tray; shallow condensate channel around the tray, removable wick, discharge openings at guide-duct lower ends, pull tab accessible with the tray out, replacement without opening a cassette; mechanical exposure indicator visible from outside with stem thermally coupled to one cassette, temperature-responsive latch, spring, latched exposed position surviving recovery, manual reset only after opening, and no control of airflow; the Operation sequence; and the optional-feature statement. Claim 5 traces to "conditioned cassettes are fitted to the spacer frame"; claim 15 traces to a depending rib entering a channel from above.

Internal consistency checks that passed: claims, Summary, Abstract and Detailed Description use the same terms and relationships as the disclosure (aligned/overlap, registered position, lower return passage, side supply passages); every numeral in draft/numerals.md is used once and for one part only, and tray feet 22 are kept distinct from resilient feet 58; the FIG. 1 section plane ("transversely to the two phase-change cassettes and through the mating channel") is geometrically consistent with the left/right and upper/lower placement of the FIG. 3, FIG. 4 and FIG. 5 fragments and with FIG. 2's wall assignments; the three broken-line enlargement curves carry the same designations in FIG-1.md, in the Brief Description and in each enlargement brief; the section line is designated "7-7" identically in FIG-6.md (repeated at both ends, both arrows one way), in FIG-7.md and in both Brief Description sentences, and the FIG. 7 view direction is consistent with the FIG. 6 arrow direction; no drafting note, placeholder, open question, instruction or unresolved alternative remains anywhere in draft/ or figures/. prior_art/INDEX.md lists no documents and the Background cites none, so there is nothing to trace in the citation channel; the Background's generic powered/passive-carrier characterizations need no inventor support.

Three defects found. One is critical: FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 verbalize the tray side wall's lower edge as "spaced above the floor 12 just inboard of the trough" / "spaced above the upwardly facing top surface of the horizontal bottom body immediately inboard of the trough". No inventor passage describes a lower edge, its spacing, or its position relative to the condensate channel, and the spacing opens a gap by which the side supply passage reaches the space beneath the tray without passing the perforations 30, contradicting the one disclosed route recited in claims 1, 13 and 17. The only text describing that choice is the drafting agent's own turn. findings.title: Untraced tray-wall lower-edge geometry in FIG. 1 and FIG. 5 opens an undisclosed bypass around the perforations
findings.where: figures/FIG-1.md line 7; figures/FIG-5.md line 9 (and the dependent wording in figures/FIG-4.md line 15)
findings.detail: Both briefs verbalize the level of the tray side wall's lower edge and its position relative to the condensate channel. The disclosure discloses only that the tray is "suspended above the shell floor by feet", that the side supply passages are formed between the tray side walls and the shell side walls, and that air "enters the side supply passages, passes through perforations in the product tray, and returns through the lower return passage". There is no affirmative passage describing a lower edge of the tray side wall, its spacing above the floor, or its position immediately inboard of the trough. These are relative locations on a flow boundary and are therefore substantive even in a schematic section. They also do technical work in the wrong direction: a lower edge spaced above the floor leaves an open gap by which the side supply passage 28 communicates with the space beneath the tray without passing through the perforations 30, so the depicted structure gives the perforations no function and departs from the single circulation path recited in claims 1, 13 and 17 and in draft/08-detailed-description.md line 9 ("Perforations 30 through the product tray 20 open from the side supply passages 28 into the lower return passage 24"). The only text that describes this arrangement is the drafting agent's own turn at input/conversation.md line 21, which is labeled YOU and is not inventor support.

findings.title: FIG. 2 asserts an untraced runout for the mating channel groove, and the assertion strains against FIG. 3's fit for the same groove
findings.detail: FIG. 2 states that the mating channel groove runs across the thickness of the near long side wall, i.e. that it runs out at both the inboard and the outboard face of that wall. The disclosure says only that "the rib enters a mating channel in the spacer frame and shifts the thermal module into a registered position". Nothing describes the groove's extent or its runout. Runout direction on a registration slot is expressly substantive geometry, because the directions in which the groove can constrain and shift the frame are what make the peripheral outlet openings overlap the side supply passages. The statement also constrains the same groove differently from FIG. 3, which is a section on a plane cutting across that wall and which fixes the groove's width to the rib's thickness with the two in contact; satisfying both briefs forces an undisclosed equality between the rib thickness and the side wall thickness. The Detailed Description and claim 15 are correctly shape-neutral ("opens upward at a top region of the spacer frame"), so the defect is confined to the figure brief and can be removed there.
